--- title: "[Surv]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} A survival response, built exactly as R's `survival::Surv()` builds one. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L315-L1306){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python Surv(time, time2=None, event=None, *, type=None, origin=0.0) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} `Surv()` records a time-to-event outcome in one of R's forms. The type is inferred from the arguments, as in R: - `Surv(time, event)` is right-censored. `event=` may be logical, `0`/`1`, or `1`/`2` (as in the `lung` data, where `2` means died). - `Surv(start, stop, event)` is a counting-process response, for late entry (left truncation) and time-varying covariates. - A categorical `event=` (a pandas or Polars categorical, or an Arrow dictionary) gives a multi-state response, whose first level means censored. - `type="left"`, `type="interval"`, and `type="interval2"` must be asked for. Status values R doesn't accept become missing, with a warning. Missing values are kept, and rows with any missing value are dropped when a model is fitted. For exact, right-, left-, and interval-censored data, `event_time()` is often clearer, and `as_surv()` converts it. `Surv()` takes values: lists, arrays, or series already in hand. To start from a data frame, name the columns instead, in a formula such as `"Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age"` or with `Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2")`, and pass `data=` when fitting. That form is evaluated on the frame's own backend, so it works the same on pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB, and lazy frames. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [time]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Follow-up time for right-censored data, or the start time for counting-process data, or the lower bound for interval data. Numeric, with `None` or `nan` for missing values. [time2]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Stop time for counting-process data, or the upper bound for interval data. When `event=` is not given and `type=` is not an interval type, a second argument is the status (R's rule), so `Surv(time, status)` works positionally. [event]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The status. Logical, `0`/`1`, or `1`/`2` for right, left, and counting data. Codes `0` (right), `1` (exact), `2` (left), and `3` (interval) for `type="interval"`. A categorical for a multi-state response. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of `"right"`, `"left"`, `"interval"`, `"counting"`, `"interval2"`, or `"mstate"`. The default infers `"right"` or `"counting"` from the number of arguments. [origin]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Subtracted from every time, as in R. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a time or the status isn't of a type R accepts. The messages match R's. [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If lengths differ, or the arguments don't fit the requested type. ::: ## Warns {.doc-warns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [UserWarning]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : When status values are invalid or intervals run backwards. Those rows become missing, as in R. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Four subjects: events at times 5 and 4, censored at 6 and 9: ::: {#1927f501 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` Surv(type=right, n=4, events=2) ``` ::: ::: `1`/`2` status coding works as it does in R, where `2` means an event: ::: {#b57d467c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[2, 1, 2, 1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` Surv(type=right, n=4, events=2) ``` ::: ::: A start time gives a counting-process response: ::: {#9fb9f866 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Surv(type=counting, n=3, events=2) ``` ::: ::: A categorical status gives a multi-state response, with the first level meaning censored: ::: {#e8ba0aef .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd outcome = pd.Categorical( ["death", "censor", "relapse", "death"], categories=["censor", "relapse", "death"] ) gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8], event=outcome) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Surv(type=mright, n=4, events=3, states=('relapse', 'death')) ``` ::: ::: Interval data uses R's coding, or lower and upper bounds with `type="interval2"`: ::: {#04d3a14e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np # The event happened in (1, 2], after 2, and in (3, 5] gw.Surv(time=[1, 2, 3], time2=[2, np.inf, 5], type="interval2") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` Surv(type=interval, n=3, events=2) ``` ::: ::: Starting from a data frame, name the columns and let the model read them. We'll use the bundled `pbc` dataset, from a Mayo Clinic trial in primary biliary cholangitis, where status is `0` (censored), `1` (transplant), or `2` (died): ::: {#a22074e1 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pbc = gw.load_dataset("pbc") # The same as Surv(time, status == 2) in R, evaluated on the frame's own backend gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age + bili", data=pbc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` CoxPH (Cox proportional hazards model, ties='efron') coef exp(coef) se(coef) z p age 0.04313 1.044 0.008055 5.354 8.594e-08 bili 0.1436 1.154 0.01142 12.578 2.8e-36 n = 418, events = 161 Likelihood ratio test = 126.1 on 2 df, p = 4.097e-28 ``` ::: ::: ## Attributes {.doc-attributes}
Name Description
entry The time each row enters the risk set, defined for every type.
event Whether each row ended in an event, as a boolean array.
is_multistate Whether the response has more than one kind of event.
is_truncated Whether the response has start times (late entry or time-varying data).
lower The first time column of interval data (R's `time1`), otherwise `None`.
n The number of rows, including any with missing values.
n_censored The number of censored rows (status `0`).
n_events The number of rows that ended in an event.
start The time each row starts being at risk, for counting-process data.
states The names of the event states of a multi-state response, otherwise `None`.
status The status column, one code per row, stored as floats as R stores it.
stop The main time column, one value per row.
type The kind of response, using R's type names.
### [entry]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The time each row enters the risk set, defined for every type. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [entry]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [FloatArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} For counting-process data this is the start time of each interval, the same as `start`. For every other type, subjects are at risk from the beginning, so every value is minus infinity (`-inf`). Estimators use `entry` to build risk sets without having to check whether the response has start times. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#b7fbf7d3 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]).entry ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([-inf, -inf]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#23175425 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} gw.Surv(time=[0, 2], time2=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]).entry ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array([0., 2.]) ``` ::: ::: ### [event]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether each row ended in an event, as a boolean array. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [event]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [npt.NDArray[np.bool_]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} A row counts as an event when its status is `1` or more. For multi-state data that means any state, not a particular one. For interval data it means the event is known to have happened (exactly, before a time, or within an interval), so only right-censored rows are `False`. Rows with a missing status are `False`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#36255e08 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]).event ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` array([ True, False, True, False]) ``` ::: ::: ### [is_multistate]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether the response has more than one kind of event. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [is_multistate]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} `True` for multi-state and competing-risks responses (types `MRIGHT` and `MCOUNTING`), which come from a categorical `event=` or from `first_event()`. Their state names are in `states`. Estimators for a single event type, such as `KaplanMeier` and `CoxPH`, reject these responses. Competing-risks estimators such as `AalenJohansen` require them. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#67c787e6 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import greenwood as gw outcome = pd.Categorical(["pcm", "censor"], categories=["censor", "pcm", "death"]) gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=outcome).is_multistate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ### [is_truncated]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether the response has start times (late entry or time-varying data). ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [is_truncated]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} `True` for counting-process responses, built as `Surv(time=start, time2=stop, event=...)`, including multi-state ones. Estimators that can't handle delayed entry check this and raise an error rather than silently ignoring the start times. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#499e66db .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[0, 2], time2=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]).is_truncated ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ### [lower]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The first time column of interval data (R's `time1`), otherwise `None`. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [lower]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [FloatArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} For interval data this is the time that goes with each row's status: the censoring time for right-censored rows, the event time for exact rows, the time by which the event had happened for left-censored rows, and the lower bound for interval-censored rows (whose upper bound is in `stop`). For every other type it is `None`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#fa7e764b .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import greenwood as gw # Rows: an interval (1, 2], right-censored at 2, an interval (3, 5] y = gw.Surv(time=[1, 2, 3], time2=[2, np.inf, 5], type="interval2") y.lower, y.stop, y.status ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` (array([1., 2., 3.]), array([2., 1., 5.]), array([3., 0., 3.])) ``` ::: ::: ### [n]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The number of rows, including any with missing values. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} Each row is one observation: one subject for most data, or one interval of a subject's follow-up for counting-process data. Rows with missing values are counted here but dropped when a model is fitted, so a fit may use fewer rows. `len(y)` gives the same number. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#36e42e53 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]).n ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: ### [n_censored]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The number of censored rows (status `0`). ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [n_censored]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} For right, counting, and multi-state data these are the rows that were event-free when last seen. For left data, status `0` means left-censored, and for interval data it means right-censored. Rows with a missing status are not counted, so `n_events + n_censored` is less than `n` when some statuses are missing. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#47d1f183 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]) y.n_censored, y.n_events + y.n_censored == y.n ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` (2, True) ``` ::: ::: ### [n_events]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The number of rows that ended in an event. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [n_events]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} This counts the `True` values of `event`: rows with status `1` or more, in any state for multi-state data. Rows with a missing status are not counted. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#22552d5b .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]).n_events ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: ### [start]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The time each row starts being at risk, for counting-process data. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [start]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [FloatArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} A counting-process response, `Surv(time=start, time2=stop, event=...)`, describes each row as an interval `(start, stop]`. This is how late entry (left truncation) and time-varying covariates are expressed. A row whose start is not before its stop has its start set to `nan`, with a warning, as in R. For every other type there are no start times and this is `None`. Use `entry` for a value that is defined for every type. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#9ff088b9 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw # Subject 2 joins the study at time 2 gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]).start ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` array([0., 2., 1.]) ``` ::: ::: ### [states]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The names of the event states of a multi-state response, otherwise `None`. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [states]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [tuple[str, ...] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} A multi-state response comes from a categorical `event=` (or `first_event()`). Its first category means censored, and the remaining categories, in order, are the states. A row with status `k` reached `states[k - 1]`. For single-event responses this is `None`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#b979aca5 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import greenwood as gw outcome = pd.Categorical( ["death", "censor", "relapse"], categories=["censor", "relapse", "death"] ) y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7], event=outcome) y.states, y.status ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` (('relapse', 'death'), array([2., 0., 1.])) ``` ::: ::: ### [status]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The status column, one code per row, stored as floats as R stores it. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [status]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [FloatArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} The codes depend on the type: - Right and counting data: `1` for an event, `0` for censored. Logical status and R's `1`/`2` coding are converted to these codes when the response is built. - Left data: `1` for an exact event, `0` for left-censored. - Interval data: `0` right-censored, `1` exact, `2` left-censored, `3` interval-censored. - Multi-state data: `0` for censored, `k` for the `k`-th entry of `states`. Codes that R doesn't accept become missing (`nan`) when the response is built, with a warning, as do backwards intervals. Use `int(y.status[i])` when a code is used as an index. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} R's `1`/`2` coding (as in the `lung` data) becomes `0`/`1`: ::: {#9a19b04b .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4], event=[2, 1, 2]).status ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` array([1., 0., 1.]) ``` ::: ::: ### [stop]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The main time column, one value per row. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [stop]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [FloatArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} What it holds depends on the type, following R's `Surv` matrix: - Right, left, and multi-state data: the follow-up time (R's time column). - Counting-process data: the time each interval ends (R's stop column). - Interval data: the upper bound (R's time2 column). As in R, rows that are not interval-censored (status other than `3`) hold the placeholder `1`, and their time is in `lower`. Any origin offset given to `Surv(origin=...)` has already been subtracted. Missing times are `nan`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#e03050d7 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]).stop ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` array([5., 6., 4., 9.]) ``` ::: ::: ### [type]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} The kind of response, using R's type names. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [CensoringType]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} One of `CensoringType.RIGHT`, `LEFT`, `INTERVAL`, `COUNTING`, `MRIGHT` (multi-state), or `MCOUNTING` (multi-state with start times). The type is chosen when the response is built: inferred from the arguments, as in R, or set with `type=`. A `type="interval2"` response reports `INTERVAL`, because R converts it to interval coding. Because `CensoringType` is a `str` enum, the value also compares equal to R's type strings. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#9da65e58 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]) y.type, y.type == "counting" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` (, True) ``` ::: ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
\__getitem__() Select rows, returning a new response of the same type.
from_dict() Rebuild a response from the output of `~~greenwood.Surv.to_dict()`.
from_json() Rebuild a response from the output of `~~greenwood.Surv.to_json()`.
is_na() Return which rows have a missing value in any column, as R's `is.na()` does.
to_dict() Return a JSON-ready mapping that fully describes the response.
to_frame() Return the response as a table with the same columns as R's `Surv` matrix.
to_json() Serialize the response to a JSON string.
### [\__getitem__()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Select rows, returning a new response of the same type. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1006-L1070){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python __getitem__(key) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Indexing works like indexing a NumPy array and always returns a `Surv`, even for a single row (as subsetting an R `Surv` with `y[i]` does). Every column is subset together, and the type and state names are kept. Negative integers count from the end, as usual in Python. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [key]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : An integer, a slice, an array of integer positions, or a boolean mask with one value per row. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Surv]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The selected rows. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [IndexError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If an integer position is out of range. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `key` is not an integer, a slice, an integer array, or a boolean mask. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#e5cc8a77 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]) y[1:3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` Surv(type=right, n=2, events=1) ``` ::: ::: A boolean mask keeps the rows where it is `True`, here the events: ::: {#e498655b .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} y[y.event] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` Surv(type=right, n=2, events=2) ``` ::: ::: ### [from_dict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Rebuild a response from the output of `~~greenwood.Surv.to_dict()`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1186-L1243){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python from_dict(data) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The mapping is read as it was written, without applying `Surv()`'s rules again: the stored type, columns, and state names are used directly. The result compares equal to the response that produced the mapping. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [data]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Mapping[str, Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A mapping produced by `~~greenwood.Surv.to_dict()`, possibly after a round trip through JSON. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Surv]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The rebuilt response. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the mapping has an unsupported layout version, such as one written by an earlier Greenwood release. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#4c627dd0 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]) data = y.to_dict() gw.Surv.from_dict(data) == y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ### [from_json()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Rebuild a response from the output of `~~greenwood.Surv.to_json()`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1273-L1306){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python from_json(text) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The text is parsed with `json.loads()` and passed to `~~greenwood.Surv.from_dict()`, so the same rules apply: the stored type, columns, and state names are used as they are, and the result compares equal to the response that was serialized. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [text]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A JSON string produced by `~~greenwood.Surv.to_json()`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Surv]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The rebuilt response. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the text is not valid JSON, or has an unsupported layout version. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#f9472a11 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]) text = y.to_json() gw.Surv.from_json(text) == y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ### [is_na()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Return which rows have a missing value in any column, as R's `is.na()` does. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L964-L999){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python is_na() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A row is missing when any of its columns is `nan`: a missing time, a missing status, or (for counting data) a missing start time. `Surv()` keeps such rows rather than dropping them, as R does. They come from missing input values, and also from values R turns into missing when the response is built: an invalid status code, a start time that is not before its stop time, or an interval that runs backwards. Estimators drop these rows when fitting and report how many in `n_dropped_`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [numpy.ndarray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A boolean array with one value per row, `True` where the row has a missing value. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} The second subject's time is missing: ::: {#c4081be8 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv(time=[5, None, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]) y.is_na() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` array([False, True, False]) ``` ::: ::: Select the complete rows with the inverted mask: ::: {#6cb26420 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} y[~y.is_na()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` Surv(type=right, n=2, events=2) ``` ::: ::: ### [to_dict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Return a JSON-ready mapping that fully describes the response. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1156-L1184){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python to_dict() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The mapping holds only plain Python values (strings, floats, lists, and `None`), so it can be written with `json.dumps()`, stored, or sent to another process, and turned back into an equal response with `~~greenwood.Surv.from_dict()`. Missing values become `None`. The layout is versioned: version 2 stores R's `Surv` columns. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A mapping with the keys `"version"` (the layout version), `"type"` (the response type, as one of R's type names), `"states"` (the state names, or `None`), and `"columns"` (R's column names mapped to lists of values). ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#a1112f23 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]).to_dict() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` {'version': 2, 'type': 'right', 'states': None, 'columns': {'time': [5.0, 6.0], 'status': [1.0, 0.0]}} ``` ::: ::: ### [to_frame()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Return the response as a table with the same columns as R's `Surv` matrix. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1105-L1154){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python to_frame(*, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Each row of the table is one row of the response. The columns depend on the type, and match the columns of the matrix R's `Surv()` returns: - Right, left, and multi-state data: `time` and `status`. - Counting-process data: `start`, `stop`, and `status`. - Interval data: `time1`, `time2`, and `status`. As in R, `time2` is `1` for rows that are not interval-censored. Status is stored as a float, as in R. Missing values are nulls. Use this table to inspect a response, to join it back onto other data, or to export it. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Output format: `None` (default), `"pandas"`, `"polars"`, or `"pyarrow"`. When `None`, a backend is auto-detected (Polars, then Pandas, then PyArrow). ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pandas.DataFrame, polars.DataFrame, or pyarrow.Table]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One row per observation, with the columns listed above. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ImportError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the requested DataFrame library (or, with `format=None`, any of them) is not installed. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#9ff8e52e .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]).to_frame(format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### [to_json()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Serialize the response to a JSON string. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_surv.py#L1245-L1271){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python to_json(*, indent=2) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The string is the JSON encoding of `~~greenwood.Surv.to_dict()`: the layout version, the type, the state names, and R's columns, with missing values as `null`. Turn it back into a response with `~~greenwood.Surv.from_json()`. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [indent]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Indentation passed to `json.dumps()`. The default `2` is readable, and `None` gives a compact single-line string. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The JSON text. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#8e2ecea0 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw print(gw.Surv(time=[5, 6], event=[1, 0]).to_json(indent=None)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {"version": 2, "type": "right", "states": null, "columns": {"time": [5.0, 6.0], "status": [1.0, 0.0]}} ``` ::: :::
